profile.summary: This benchmark asks a model to predict the binding affinity of a drug-target pair as a number, on the two kinase affinity data sets used by the DeepDTA paper: Davis, with dissociation constants for 442 proteins and 68 ligands, and KIBA, with combined kinase inhibitor bioactivities for 229 proteins and 2111 drugs. The DeepDTA authors split each data set into six equal parts, held one part out as an independent test set, and used the remaining five parts for five-fold cross validation, and they publish those fold files so that later methods can train and test on the same pairs. It is used by people comparing drug-target affinity regression methods, including methods that read only the protein sequence and the compound SMILES string.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Materials and Methods (Data sets), Experiment Setup; data/README.md: Train and test folds

summary_quotes.text: In this study, we propose a deep-learning based model that uses only sequence information of both targets and drugs to predict DT interaction binding affinities.
It comprises interactions of 442 proteins and 68 ligands.
filtered it to contain only drugs and targets with at least 10 interactions yielding a total of 229 unique proteins and 2111 unique drugs.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is regression: given a drug and a protein target, predict how strongly they bind. The authors argue this is more informative than the binary interaction prediction that earlier work used, because binding strength is continuous and because a binary data set has to invent negative examples. Both data sets are kinase data, so the question is how well a method ranks and estimates affinities across a protein family and a library of inhibitors. The paper's own interest is whether sequence alone is enough: it compares models that read raw protein sequences and SMILES strings against models given precomputed Smith-Waterman protein similarity and PubChem compound similarity.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Materials and Methods (Data sets); Results

quotes.text: However, protein-ligand interactions assume a continuum of binding strength values, also called binding affinity and predicting this value still remains a challenge.
The lack of true-negative samples and how the study generates synthetic negative samples usually affects the performance of the prediction algorithms.
The Smith-Waterman (S-W) and Pubchem Sim algorithms were used to compute the pairwise similarities for the proteins and ligands, respectively.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Davis holds selectivity assays of kinases and their inhibitors with dissociation constants, as interactions of 442 proteins and 68 ligands, 30056 interactions in the form used here. The authors convert the Kd values to a log scale, pKd. They note that the peak at pKd 5 covers more than half of Davis, 20931 of 30056 values, and that these are pairs with very weak affinity or not seen in the primary screen. KIBA combines kinase inhibitor bioactivities from Ki, Kd and IC50 measurements into a single KIBA score; it originally covered 467 targets and 52498 drugs and was filtered by earlier work to drugs and targets with at least 10 interactions, leaving 229 proteins and 2111 drugs and 118254 interactions. Compound SMILES strings come from PubChem and protein sequences from UniProt. Each data set is stored as an affinity matrix with the pairs that have a measurement, and the published fold files hold positions in that matrix: one test fold shared by all five training sets, and five training folds. The data folder also ships drug-drug similarities from PubChem structure clustering and target-target Smith-Waterman similarities, which were used to reproduce the comparison methods.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method predicts an affinity value for every pair in the test fold. The headline metric is the Concordance Index, which asks whether two randomly chosen pairs are predicted in the same order as their measured affinities, so higher is better. Mean squared error is also reported, where lower is better. The authors fix hyper-parameters by five-fold cross validation on the five training folds, then train the chosen configuration five times, each time on four of the five training folds combined (the cross validation training set, leaving out that round's validation fold), score each of those five models on the same held-out test fold, and report the average with the standard deviation in parentheses. Significance between methods is tested with a paired t test at a 95% confidence interval. The comparison is made fair by giving the baselines the same train and test folds. The repository's own script follows this: it reads the test set and the outer training sets, uses get_cindex as the performance measure, trains with a mean squared error loss, and prints the per-fold test Concordance Index and mean squared error along with their average and standard deviation.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository, install the Python, Keras and TensorFlow versions the README lists, place the data folder under the source directory, and run run_experiments.py with the window sizes, batch size, epoch count, sequence and SMILES length limits and the dataset path for the data set you want. The README's example uses the KIBA data path and problem type 1. The script loads the affinity matrix, finds the positions that have a measurement, reads the published test and training folds, searches the given filter combinations by cross validation, retrains on each of the five four-fold training sets and logs the test Concordance Index and mean squared error.

facts.value: Two kinase affinity data sets as used by DeepDTA. Davis, with Kd values, 442 proteins, 68 compounds and 30056 interactions. KIBA, with KIBA scores, 229 proteins, 2111 compounds and 118254 interactions, after earlier work filtered the original 467 targets and 52498 drugs to those with at least 10 interactions.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: A random one in six holdout, the same for both data sets. The pairs are divided at random into six equal parts, one part is the independent test set, and the other five parts are the training folds used for five-fold cross validation to choose hyper-parameters. The published fold files give the test fold and the five training folds, and the test fold is the same for all five training sets. Counting the entries of the saved fold files gives 5010 test pairs for Davis and 19709 for KIBA.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: KronRLS and SimBoost, both given Smith-Waterman protein similarity and PubChem compound similarity. On Davis the paper reports CI 0.871 for KronRLS and 0.872 for SimBoost; on KIBA, 0.782 and 0.836. DeepDTA variants that replace one or both similarity inputs with a convolutional block are also reported, the combined model reaching CI 0.878 on Davis and 0.863 on KIBA.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None beyond the random split: the pairs are divided at random, so the same drug and the same protein appear in both training and test folds. The authors do not apply a sequence identity cut-off; they report similarity statistics for the data sets instead, that Smith-Waterman similarity between proteins is at most 60 per cent for 99 per cent of KIBA protein pairs and for 92 per cent of Davis protein pairs, and call both data sets non-redundant.

quotes.text: We should also note that the Smith-Waterman (S-W) similarity among proteins of the KIBA data set is at most 60% for 99% of the protein pairs. The target similarity is at most 60% for 92% of the protein pairs for the Davis data set. These statistics indicate that both data sets are non-redundant.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training on the benchmark's own training folds. Hyper-parameters are chosen by five-fold cross validation within the training parts, then a model is trained from those parameters five times, each time on four of the five training folds combined, and scored on the held-out test fold. The saved files describe no zero-shot or probing setting.

quotes.text: we evaluated the performance over the independent test set, when the model was trained with the learned parameters in Table 2 on the five training sets that we used in five-fold cross validation (note that the validation sets were not used).
The hyper-parameter combination that provided the best average CI score over the validation set was selected as the best combination in order to model the test set.

strengths.text: The folds are published, so a later method can train and test on exactly the same drug-target pairs. The DeepDTA authors state they gave their baselines the same train and test folds for the comparison.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup; data/README.md: Train and test folds

quotes.text: We provide the train and test folds of the data sets (https://github.com/hkmztrk/DeepDTA/).
The same setting with the same train and test folds was used for KronRLS [47] and Simboost [29] for a fair comparison.

strengths.text: Affinity is scored as a continuous value, which avoids the invented negative examples that the authors describe as a problem for binary interaction data sets.

quotes.text: formulating the DT prediction task as a binding affinity prediction problem enables the creation of more realistic data sets, where the binding affinity scores are directly used, obviating the need for the generation of synthetic negative samples.

strengths.text: Results are reported as an average over five training runs with a standard deviation, and method differences are tested with a paired t test rather than read off a single run.

strengths.text: Only sequence level inputs are needed, so the benchmark is open to methods that cannot use a protein-ligand complex structure. The authors note that structure based scoring is limited to the complexes in the PDB.

quotes.text: However, this approach is limited to known protein-ligand complex structures, with only 25000 ligands reported in PDB [49].

limitations.text: The split is random over pairs, so a drug or a protein in the test fold can also appear in training. The benchmark as published does not hold out unseen drugs or unseen targets, and the authors name prediction for novel targets and novel pairs as future work.

quotes.text: we randomly divided our data set into six equal parts in which one part is selected as the independent test set.
The methodology can then be extended to predict the affinity of known compounds/targets to novel targets/drugs as well as to the prediction of the affinity of novel drug-target pairs.

limitations.text: Davis is dominated by one value. The authors report that the peak at pKd 5 is more than half the data set, 20931 of 30056 pairs, and that these are weak or unobserved pairs, so both the metrics and the apparent differences between methods are driven by a large block of near-identical labels.

quotes.text: The peak at pKd value 5 (10000nM ) constitutes more than half of the data set (20931 out of 30056). These values correspond to the negative pairs that either have very weak binding affinities (Kd > 10000nM ) or are not observed in the primary screen [47].

limitations.text: Both data sets are kinases and their inhibitors, so a score here says nothing about other protein families. The labels are also not one assay: KIBA scores merge Ki, Kd and IC50 measurements from different sources.

quotes.text: The Davis data set contains selectivity assays of the kinase protein family and the relevant inhibitors
in which kinase inhibitor bioactivities from different sources such as Ki , Kd , and IC50 were combined [54].

limitations.text: There is no leaderboard and no licence. The saved repository files state no licence for the code or the data, and the only published result is the paper's own tables, so a new score has to be produced by rerunning the comparison methods or taken from those tables. The code also pins old versions, Python 3.4 or later with Keras 2 and TensorFlow 1.

run_guide.summary: Get the DeepDTA code and folds, install the listed dependencies, and run the training and evaluation script on one of the two data sets.
prerequisites: Python 3.4 or later, Keras 2.x, TensorFlow 1.x, numpy, matplotlib and scikit-learn, as the README lists. A conda environment file, deepdta.yml, is in the repository and the README says it was tested on Linux.
The data folder from the repository, placed under the source directory.
No licence is stated for the code or the data in the saved repository files, so check the terms before reuse.
